heard.who: Nur Masalha, historian, "Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History"
heard.quote: the name took on its Greek form Παλαιστίνη (Palaistinê or Phalastin) and was used as the name of the region

answer: The name is old but was not continuous. It comes from the Philistines (Egyptian Peleset), and Herodotus used Palaistine in the 5th century BCE for the coast between Phoenicia and Egypt. Rome combined its province of Judaea into Syria Palaestina around the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135 CE). The Byzantines had Palaestina Prima and Secunda, and the early caliphs a district called Jund Filastin. Under the Ottomans no province carried the name. Britain's Mandate of 1920-22 revived it, and Jews and Arabs alike held Palestinian citizenship. Jews and Judaea were not erased from the sources. Why Rome chose the name is not recorded: historians differ on whether it was meant to cut the Jews' tie to the land.

facts.text: The name has an ancient root: the Peleset of Egyptian texts under Ramesses III (about 1175 BCE), generally identified with the Philistines, and the Assyrian Palashtu, are the source of the later name Palestine.

contested: Why Rome renamed the province is disputed. Many writers say the aim was to sever Jewish ties to the land (Louis Feldman, "Some Observations on the Name of Palestine", 1990, says the aim was to "obliterate the Jewish character of the land"; Werner Eck also treats the renaming as punishment). David Jacobson argues it was a rational administrative choice with ancient precedent, since Palaistine already meant the wider land. Spencer McDaniel says no ancient source states a motive, calls a punitive motive plausible but unproven, and notes it may have been dated before the revolt. Eck suggests the name may have been proposed by non-Jewish provincials.

Palestine as a broad regional name is old, but what it covered varies by author: some Greek texts use it for the coast, Herodotus uses it for the wider land. Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus mostly kept Judaea for the Jewish heartland and Palestine for the coast (Feldman).

Nur Masalha argues Palestine was the commonest name for the land from the Late Bronze Age on; others treat Judaea or Land of Israel as the usual name in Jewish texts. The Ottoman state used Filastin informally on maps without making it a province.
The date of the renaming is uncertain: Eck dates an inscription to 136, and Ronald Syme and others have argued for a date near Hadrian's visit of 130 (McDaniel).

not_claimed: This card does not say Palestine is not a real place, or that Palestinians are not a people.
It does not say Jews or Arabs have a better claim because of a name.
It does not claim Hadrian's renaming was or was not meant to erase Jewish ties; it says the sources do not tell us.
It does not claim there was no Arab or Muslim population: it covers the name, not who lived in the land.
